record.paper_title: On Open Problems in Biological Network Visualization
record.original_question: Given a huge biological network with thousands of nodes and edges that is organized hierarchically into pathways and subpathways, and given selected subsets G1,...,Gk such as pathways that may overlap and may have pre-specified internal layouts or relative positions, how can one provide biologically meaningful visualization and navigation among the subsets and their interrelations? The method should support overview or backbone abstractions, interactive movement from one set of pathways to connected or related pathways, small layout changes after user interaction, appropriate context information, expand-and-collapse operations restricted to semantically meaningful structures such as pathways, preservation of drawing conventions and mental maps, and a clear treatment of duplicate biological components when overlapping subsets represent the same entity.

evidence.quote: Given a huge biological network, methods for the biologically meaningful visualization of selected subsets G1,...,Gk (e.g., pathways) and their interrelations, as well as techniques for the navigation within the network are needed.
Expand-and-collapse mechanisms thus need to be incorporated into layout algorithms such that drawing conventions and the mental map are preserved.
The subsets G1,...,Gk do not need to be disjoint but may partially overlap. This poses an additional challenge for the visualization problem

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let G = (V, E) be a very large graph (with up to thousands of vertices and edges) representing a biological network, equipped with a hierarchical decomposition H whose nodes correspond to semantically meaningful substructures (pathways and subpathways). Let G_1, …, G_k be designated subgraphs of G (e.g., pathways), which need not be pairwise disjoint: a vertex v may belong to several G_i, in which case the multiple occurrences represent the same biological entity. Some of the G_i may come with a prescribed internal layout or with prescribed relative positions to other G_j.

Develop a visualization and navigation framework, i.e., an algorithm that produces a sequence of drawings of G (and of subsystems of the G_i) together with interactive operations, satisfying all of the following requirements:

1. Overview/backbone abstraction: produce a readable abstracted drawing summarizing the G_i and the interrelations (edges of G between different G_i, and shared vertices among overlapping G_i).
2. Navigation: support interactive transitions from a currently displayed set of subsets G_{i_1}, …, G_{i_r} to a related set (e.g., neighboring or connected pathways), with smooth visual continuity.
3. Stability: after each user interaction the drawing should change only locally and minimally (mental-map preservation), and prescribed drawing conventions for biological networks and prescribed internal layouts of the G_i must be respected.
4. Expand-and-collapse: support expand and collapse operations, but only along the hierarchical decomposition H (i.e., only semantically meaningful substructures may be collapsed), and integrate these operations into the layout algorithm while preserving the conventions and mental map.
5. Context: while focusing on certain G_i, provide appropriate contextual information about the surrounding network.
6. Duplicates: provide a principled visual treatment of vertices that occur in several overlapping G_i, making clear when distinct on-screen occurrences represent the same biological entity.

Provide such a framework, prove guarantees on the layouts it produces (readability, stability under interaction, and complexity), and demonstrate its applicability to biological networks of the stated scale.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a broadly stated visualization challenge combining hierarchical graph drawing, overlapping clusters, expand/collapse with mental-map preservation, and duplicate-node handling. While partial tools exist (e.g., Cytoscape, VANTED, SBGN-compliant layouts, and work on clustered/compound graph drawing), no single framework is known to satisfy all the listed requirements simultaneously with theoretical guarantees, and the problem is generally treated as an ongoing open challenge in the bio-network visualization literature.

status_evidence.title: On Open Problems in Biological Network Visualization
status_evidence.snippet: Lists biologically meaningful visualization and navigation of overlapping pathway subsets, expand-and-collapse respecting mental map, and duplicate handling as open problems.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is posed as an open challenge in biological network visualization.
